**NTSB Rules Out Mechanical Failure in Continental Airlines Denver Runway Accident**

**DENVER** — Federal investigators probing the dramatic runway excursion of a Continental Airlines jet at Denver International Airport have largely ruled out mechanical failure as the primary cause of the crash, officials with the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) announced.

The incident occurred during takeoff when the Boeing 737 suddenly veered off the left side of the runway, skidding across an embankment before coming to a stop in a ravine and catching fire. Emergency responders quickly arrived on the scene, assisting passengers and crew as they evacuated via emergency slides. While dozens of passengers were treated for injuries ranging from minor cuts to severe fractures, all occupants survived.

To determine why the aircraft departed the runway during its takeoff roll, NTSB officials launched an intensive, multi-faceted investigation. Teams of safety inspectors conducted a meticulous physical examination of the wreckage, which had been severely damaged by impact forces and post-crash fire. Concurrently, investigators conducted detailed interviews with the flight crew, including the captain and first officer, to reconstruct the final seconds leading up to the accident and understand the cockpit dynamics.

Preliminary findings released by the board have significantly shifted the direction of the inquiry. Careful forensic analysis of the plane's critical ground systems revealed no evidence of pre-existing malfunctions. Investigators confirmed that the aircraft’s landing gear, main tires, and braking assemblies were fully operational prior to the impact. 

These findings directly contradict initial reports and early speculation that a blown tire, locked brake, or steering mechanism failure had dragged the jet off course. 

"Our examination of the hardware indicates that the airplane's ground control systems were functioning as designed up until the point of departure from the runway," said a lead NTSB investigator. "At this stage, we can comfortably rule out a pre-existing mechanical failure in the gear, tires, or brakes."

With mechanical issues largely eliminated from the equation, the NTSB has pivoted its focus toward environmental and operational factors. Investigators are currently examining the impact of strong, localized wind gusts—specifically crosswinds off the Rocky Mountains—that were reported in the area at the time of takeoff. Additionally, experts are analyzing the flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) to evaluate pilot inputs, rudder control responses, and air traffic control communications.

**NTSB probes fierce crosswinds, black boxes in terrifying Denver plane crash**

By **CNN Staff**
December 22, 2008

**(CNN)** — Federal investigators are focusing on powerful mountain wind gusts and flight control systems as they piece together how a Houston-bound Continental Airlines jet veered off a runway in Denver, plunged into a ravine, and burst into flames.

Miraculously, all 110 passengers and five crew members survived the Saturday night crash of Flight 1404 at Denver International Airport, though 38 people suffered injuries, including broken bones and severe burns.

As snow began to fall over the charred wreckage of the Boeing 737-500 on Sunday, officials from the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) arrived on the scene to begin what they caution will be a lengthy investigation into one of the most dramatic aviation survivals in recent memory.

[VIDEO PLACEHOLDER: NTSB briefing on Denver airport crash investigation]

### NTSB Focuses on Wind, Runway Evidence

Speaking at a press briefing at the airport, NTSB Board Member Robert Sumwalt said investigators are looking closely at extreme weather conditions present at the time of the 6:18 p.m. takeoff roll. 

"We are looking at everything—the weather, the aircraft, the human component, and the runway conditions," Sumwalt said. "The fact that there were no fatalities in an accident of this magnitude is truly remarkable, but our job now is to figure out exactly why this airplane left the runway."

Sumwalt confirmed that wind gusts of up to 45 knots (approx. 51 mph) were reported in the area around the time Flight 1404 attempted to take off on Runway 34L. 

Initial ground evidence indicates the aircraft departed the left side of the runway approximately 2,600 feet into its takeoff roll, traveling across snow-covered grass before dropping into a 40-foot ravine. The impact sheared off the plane's landing gear and right engine, triggering a intense fire that gutted the right side of the fuselage.

Sumwalt stated that both the Cockpit Voice Recorder (CVR) and the Flight Data Recorder (FDR)—the so-called "black boxes"—have been recovered and sent to the NTSB laboratories in Washington, D.C., for immediate analysis. 

"We hope to extract clear data that will tell us the aircraft's speed, heading, control surface movements, and engine output right up to the moment of impact," Sumwalt added.

[VIDEO PLACEHOLDER: Wreckage of Continental Flight 1404 seen in daytime light]

### 'Pure Chaos': Passengers Recall Escape

For those inside the cabin, the routine takeoff rapidly devolved into horror. Passengers described a violent shuddering followed by a sudden, sharp left turn as the jet lost directional control.

"It felt like a severe roller coaster, and then suddenly we were off the paved road and hitting massive bumps," said passenger Gabriel Trejos, who was traveling home for the holidays. "Then came a huge jolt, and the right side of the plane just burst into flames. People were screaming, smoke was filling the cabin instantly. It was pure chaos."

Despite the thick black smoke and intense heat melting the interior plastic, passengers moved quickly toward the emergency exits.

"I opened my eyes and saw fire right outside my window," recalled Emily Pellegrini, another survivor. "The flight attendants were yelling for everyone to get down and get out. People were climbing over seats to reach the left-side doors. It’s an absolute miracle we all crawled out of that ravine alive."

The plane's captain suffered severe back injuries in the crash, while several passengers were treated for smoke inhalation and fractures. Airport emergency crews arrived at the scene within minutes, managing to extinguish the blaze before the aircraft was entirely consumed.

[VIDEO PLACEHOLDER: Surviving passengers describe escaping burning fuselage]

### Long Road Ahead for Investigators

Operations at Denver International Airport have largely returned to normal, though Runway 34L remains closed as NTSB investigators, along with teams from Boeing, Continental Airlines, and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), document the debris field.

Sumwalt emphasized that while crosswinds are a primary line of inquiry, investigators have not ruled out mechanical failure, pilot error, or sudden surface conditions on the runway.

"We do not speculate on cause," Sumwalt said. "We follow the facts, and right now we are at the very beginning of gathering those facts."

The NTSB expects to remain on site in Denver for up to a week, with a preliminary report expected in the coming days.

---
*CNN's Sean Morris and Mike Ahlers contributed to this report.*

**NTSB Points to Severe Crosswinds in Early Investigation of Denver Continental Airlines Crash**

**DENVER** — Federal safety investigators examining the runway crash of Continental Airlines Flight 1404 at Denver International Airport (DIA) have focused their preliminary investigation on sudden, extreme crosswinds that struck the aircraft during its takeoff roll. 

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) released its early findings following an initial analysis of the aircraft's flight recorders, radar data, weather logs, and physical wreckage. 

Flight 1404, a Boeing 737-500 bound for Houston on the evening of December 20, 2008, carried 110 passengers and five crew members. While the crash resulted in severe structural damage and a localized fire, all 115 occupants survived—a outcome officials have described as extraordinary given the violent nature of the impact.

Here is a detailed breakdown of the early NTSB findings:

---

### Key Preliminary Findings

#### 1. Extreme Wind Gusts at Takeoff
* **Wind Conditions:** NTSB data reveals that as the plane accelerated down Runway 34L, it was hit by powerful, localized wind gusts from the left (west/northwest). Weather sensors near the runway recorded sustained winds around 31 knots (36 mph) with gusts reaching between 44 and 45 knots (over 50 mph).
* **Mountain Wave Phenomenon:** Investigators are evaluating whether a atmospheric phenomenon known as a "mountain wave"—strong wind currents spilling over the Rocky Mountains—created severe turbulence and localized wind shear close to the ground.

#### 2. Loss of Directional Control
* **Speed at Excursion:** The Flight Data Recorder (FDR) indicated that the aircraft was accelerating normally and had reached approximately 104 knots (120 mph) when it abruptly veered to the left, off the centerline of the runway.
* **Pilot Response:** Recorder data shows that the captain attempted to correct the leftward drift by applying full right rudder and right nose-wheel steering, along with right-side brake application. Despite these maximum control inputs, the force of the crosswind pushed the aircraft off the left side of the runway.

#### 3. No Immediate Evidence of Mechanical Failure
* **Systems Intact:** Early physical inspection of the engines, flight control surfaces, tires, and braking systems showed no signs of pre-impact failure or malfunction. 
* **Engine Power:** Both CFM56 engines were operating normally and producing symmetric thrust up until the plane left the paved surface. 
* **Tire/Brake Integrity:** Ground tracks and tire wreckage indicated that the tires were intact and the brakes were functioning prior to the plane leaving the runway.

#### 4. Wreckage Path and Structural Damage
* **Path of Destruction:** After leaving the runway, the aircraft traversed a snow-covered field, launched over a taxiway embankment, and slammed into a deep ravine containing a service road.
* **Impact Forces:** The collision with the ravine terrain sheared off the landing gear, separated the right engine, cracked the main fuselage behind the wings, and caused the tail section to drop.
* **Post-Crash Fire:** A fire broke out on the right side of the aircraft shortly after impact, fed by ruptured fuel lines near the right wing. Firefighters arrived on the scene within minutes to extinguish the blazes and assist in the evacuation.

#### 5. Evacuation and Injuries
* **Miraculous Survival:** Emergency slides were deployed on the left side of the aircraft (away from the fire). Thirty-eight people were transported to local hospitals with injuries ranging from bumps and bruises to fractures. 
* **Severe Injuries:** The captain suffered severe injuries, including broken bones, due to the collapse of the cockpit floor structure upon impact in the ravine.

---

### Next Steps in the Investigation

NTSB officials stressed that while crosswinds are currently the primary line of inquiry, the investigation remains in its early stages. 

Over the coming months, the safety board plans to:
* Conduct detailed aerodynamic simulations to determine if the crosswind speeds encountered exceeded the Boeing 737-500's maximum lateral control capabilities.
* Review Air Traffic Control (ATC) communication to assess whether the flight crew received adequate wind warning data prior to clearance for takeoff.
* Examine airport terrain features to determine if localized ground structures contributed to unusual wind turbulence on Runway 34L.
* Test components of the rudder and steering systems in laboratory settings to definitively rule out latent mechanical anomalies.

A complete final report detailing the probable cause of the crash is expected to take up to a year to complete.

**THE DENVER DAILY EXPRESS**

**CROSSWINDS AND CRUNCHED METAL: Investigators Release New Details on Continental Flight 1404 Crash**

**By Alex Mercer**  
*Senior Aviation Correspondent*  

**DENVER —** Federal safety officials revealed critical updates today regarding the harrowing crash of Continental Airlines Flight 1404, pointing to sudden, powerful crosswinds and ruling out mechanical landing gear failure prior to the moment the Boeing 737-500 veered off a Denver International Airport runway and plunged into a ravine. 

The Houston-bound jet snapped into pieces and erupted in flames on Saturday evening after swerving off Runway 37R during its takeoff roll. Miraculously, all 115 passengers and crew survived, though 38 suffered injuries, ranging from broken bones to smoke inhalation.

As the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) continues its painstaking analysis of the charred wreckage, newly released findings from the aircraft’s landing gear, the cockpit voice recorder (CVR), and harrowing testimony from survivors are offering a clearer picture of the final, terrifying seconds on the tarmac.

---

### **Landing Gear Ruled Out as Initial Cause**

Initial speculation from aviation experts suggested that a locked brake or a premature collapse of the nose wheel gear might have pulled the 90,000-pound aircraft violently to the left. However, NTSB Board Member Lead Investigator Earl Weener confirmed today that physical evidence points away from a pre-impact mechanical failure.

"Examination of the tire tracks and remaining gear components indicates the landing gear was fully operational up until the moment the aircraft exited the paved runway surface," Weener stated during a morning press briefing.

Investigators reported that both main landing gear assemblies and the nose wheel sheared off only after the plane crossed a taxiway and bounded over uneven terrain toward the 40-foot ravine. Tire marks on the runway show the aircraft maintained a straight line for roughly 1,800 feet before making a sharp, leftward turn. Tests on the jet's brake systems and steering control revealed no pre-existing defects.

Instead, meteorologists and NTSB data analysts are zeroing in on localized wind gusts. Wind sensors near Runway 37R recorded sudden crosswinds reaching up to 45 knots (51 mph) at the exact moment the plane lost control—far stronger than the steady 27-knot breeze reported to the pilots just minutes prior.

---

### **CVR Reveals Seconds of Chaos in the Cockpit**

The jet’s Cockpit Voice Recorder (CVR) has provided investigators with a vivid, second-by-second acoustic account of the crew’s struggle to maintain control. 

According to NTSB transcripts, the takeoff roll proceeded normally for the first 15 seconds. At approximately 115 knots—well below the speed required for lift-off—a loud thud and severe vibration can be heard on the recording, followed immediately by the captain exclaiming, "Left, left!" 

Audio analysis reveals the sound of engines roaring as the crew attempted to use differential thrust and heavy right-rudder pedal force to correct the drift. 

"Rudder's maxed out!" one of the pilots is heard shouting as warning chimes began sounding in the cockpit. Less than six seconds later, the recording captured the violent sound of impact as the plane hit the ravine wall, followed by the sound of the engines cutting out and the CVR’s power severing.

"The crew fought to keep that airplane on the centerline," said Captain Dan Allen, a former commercial pilot acting as an independent analyst. "When a mountain microburst hits a fast-moving aircraft laterally, even full rudder application sometimes isn't enough to prevent a slide."

---

### **Passengers Recall Darkness, Dust, and Flames**

For the 110 passengers aboard, what was supposed to be a routine evening flight to Texas turned into a sudden scene of terror. 

Gabriel Trejos, 34, sitting in row 14, described the moment the plane left the runway. 

"It felt like we hit a brick wall sideways," Trejos recalled from his hospital room, where he is being treated for minor burns. "Suddenly we were bouncing wildly over dirt and rocks. Overhead bins burst open, luggage was flying everywhere, and the noise of metal twisting was deafening."

Trejos said the right side of the cabin filled with a orange glow almost immediately after the plane came to a halt in the ravine. "People started screaming 'Fire!' I looked out the window and saw fuel burning right on the wing. It felt like we had seconds to get out."

Despite the darkness, thick smoke, and the cabin snapping in two near the rear, passengers and flight attendants orchestrated a rapid evacuation. 

Emily Vance, who was traveling with her six-year-old daughter, praised the flight crew for their quick action. "The flight attendants were yelling, 'Leave your bags! Move, move, move!' One of them literally pushed people out of the overwing exit onto the ground. The fire was growing so fast, but everyone managed to scramble up the snowy embankment."

Rescuers arrived on the scene within three minutes of the crash, fighting cold temperatures and wind-driven flames to assist survivors who were huddled together in the freezing darkness near the burning fuselage.

---

### **Next Steps in the Investigation**

NTSB crews are expected to remain at Denver International Airport for another week, clearing the wreckage piece by piece to a secure hangar for metallurgical testing. 

While the preliminary focus rests heavily on wind shear and extreme crosswinds, investigators stress that the inquiry is far from over. Over the coming months, the team will review air traffic control tapes, analyze the Flight Data Recorder (FDR) telemetry, and interview both the captain and first officer—who are currently recovering from serious injuries—to determine if airport safety protocols or wind-warning systems were sufficient.

A full, final report on the crash of Continental Flight 1404 is expected to take up to 12 months to complete.

**Miracle in the Mile High City: The Crash and Investigation of Continental Flight 1404**

On the freezing, wind-swept night of December 20, 2008, Continental Airlines Flight 1404 prepared for a routine departure from Denver International Airport (DEN) bound for George Bush Intercontinental Airport in Houston. Onboard the Boeing 737-500 were 110 passengers and five crew members. What should have been an ordinary two-hour flight transformed into seconds of terror, resulting in one of the most remarkable stories of survival in modern aviation history.

As the aircraft accelerated down Runway 34L at nearly 115 mph, a powerful gust of wind struck the plane. Flight 1404 veered violently to the left, shot off the runway, skidded across a snow-covered field and taxiway, and plunged over a 40-foot ravine. The impact sheared off the landing gear and left engine, cracking the fuselage open and igniting a fierce inferno. 

Despite the horrific destruction and the cabin rapidly filling with smoke and fire, all 115 people on board survived. Thirty-eight people suffered injuries, including fractures and burns—with the captain sustaining severe spinal injuries—but the absence of fatalities earned the incident the title of the "Denver Miracle."

### Voices from Inside the Cabin

For those inside the cabin, the transition from a standard takeoff to a fight for survival happened in the blink of an eye. 

Passenger Jeb Tilly recalled the violent, chaotic moments as the jet left the pavement. "It was just a violent ride," Tilly described after the crash, detailing how the aircraft shook violently as it bounced off the runway. "The plane just started shuddering... and then it felt like we hit a massive ditch." As the plane came to a halt in the ravine, Tilly focused entirely on escaping the wreckage as flames crept up the side of the fuselage. "I thought, 'We’ve got to get out of here right now.' It was complete instinct."

For Gabriel Trejos, who was traveling with his pregnant wife, the horror was amplified by the immediate threat of the growing fire outside his window. "I looked out the window and all I saw was fire," Trejos recalled. "It was just bright orange and red everywhere." As smoke poured into the cabin, Trejos and his wife scrambled through the darkness toward an emergency exit. Reflecting on the harrowing ordeal and the instinct to protect his family, Trejos shared the terror of those brief seconds: "You don’t know if the plane is going to explode. The only thought in your head is: 'We need to get out.'"

Thanks to the rapid actions of the flight crew, passengers like Tilly and Trejos were able to evacuate through the usable over-wing exits and doors before the fire completely engulfed the main cabin.

### Inside the Cockpit: CVR Findings

As federal investigators from the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) descended on Denver, one of their primary tasks was analyzing the Cockpit Voice Recorder (CVR) to understand the crew's actions and the sequence of events.

The CVR recording painted a dramatic picture of how quickly control was lost. The audio captured a normal, professional pre-flight routine and initial takeoff roll. The crew made standard airspeed callouts, reaching "80 knots" without issue. 

However, just 41 seconds into the takeoff roll, the audio captured the sudden onset of loud rumbling noises and severe vibration as the aircraft began to drift off course. The CVR recorded the pilots' immediate, shocked reactions as they struggled to maintain control. Sounds of the aircraft bouncing violently over the ground were accompanied by brief exclamations from the flight crew before the recording abruptly cut off upon impact. The recording confirmed that the crew had very little time—less than six seconds from the initial severe leftward drift—to react before the plane left the runway surface entirely.

### Investigating the Mechanicals: Robert Sumwalt’s Briefing

Early in the investigation, rumors swirled regarding potential mechanical failures, such as a blown tire or jammed brakes, which might have pulled the heavy jet off the center line. 

NTSB Board Member (and later Chairman) Robert Sumwalt addressed the media and public directly to clarify the physical evidence gathered from the runway and the wreckage. Sumwalt specifically highlighted the condition of the plane’s landing gear, tires, and braking systems to dispel early speculation.

Sumwalt stated that a thorough examination of the runway debris and the aircraft's physical remains showed that the tires were fully inflated and intact prior to the plane leaving the runway. "We found no evidence of any tire failure or tread separation prior to the aircraft departing the runway surface," Sumwalt explained during a press briefing, noting that tire marks on the runway indicated the rubber had remained intact during the slide.

Furthermore, Sumwalt addressed the possibility of a brake system malfunction or asymmetric braking. He confirmed that the NTSB's examination of the brake assemblies revealed "no evidence that the brakes were applied prior to the aircraft leaving the runway." Sumwalt’s comments effectively ruled out a mechanical lockup or tire blowout as the initiating cause of the crash, shifting the investigation’s core focus toward environmental factors—specifically, severe wind shear and crosswinds.

### The Final Verdict and Legacy

In July 2010, the NTSB issued its final report on Continental Flight 1404. The board determined that the probable cause of the accident was the captain's failure to apply sufficient right rudder control to counteract an intense, sudden crosswind gust. 

On the night of the crash, strong "mountain wave" winds were blowing off the Rocky Mountains, generating localized gusts of up to 45 knots (52 mph) across Runway 34L. As the wind struck the tail of the aircraft, it caused the plane to "weathercock" or pivot left into the wind. The NTSB also noted that the airport's wind detection systems did not provide real-time, localized wind shear alerts that could have warned the pilots of the severe conditions on that specific portion of the runway.

The crash of Flight 1404 led to significant safety advancements, including revised simulator training for pilots handling extreme crosswinds, improved wind-measuring equipment at major airports, and redesigns of runway safety areas to prevent planes from falling into steep ravines.

While the aircraft was completely destroyed, the miracle of Flight 1404 remains a testament to modern aircraft structural safety standards, effective cabin crew training, and the sheer luck that allowed 115 people to walk away from a blazing inferno in the Colorado night.
